title: Does Accountability Still Matter?
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin takes aim at districts replacing traditional accountability — time-out, suspensions, clearly enforced rules — with restorative-style alternatives he considers vague and ineffective. He argues district leaders can't articulate what teachers should actually do instead because, in his view, no functioning replacement exists, only euphemisms like 'communities of care' and disputed statistics about reduced suspensions. His central argument is that true accountability, where a misbehaving student loses something they want to be part of, teaches responsibility and protects every student's equal right to learn, while removing it produces predictable chaos regardless of the good intentions behind it. He frames the underlying motive as a push for equal outcomes rather than equal opportunity, and closes with a pointed rebuke of leaders who publicly champion these changes while bearing none of the resulting cost themselves.
points: Removing time-out and other traditional accountability is argued to reliably increase bullying, disrespect, and general misbehavior.
District leaders are said to be unable to specify a workable replacement because, in the author's view, no effective one exists.
True accountability — losing access to something valued — is framed as teaching responsibility, empathy, and equal protection under a single standard.
The push to remove accountability is attributed to a goal of equal outcomes for every student rather than equal opportunity.
The consequences of these policy shifts are said to fall on teachers, parents, and students, not on the leaders promoting them.
quotes: Many school districts are racing to remove student accountability. Time-out is being outlawed. Suspensions are becoming a no-no.
Remove accountability and bullying , rudeness, disrespect, and every other form of misbehavior will rise like an angry phoenix.
But they won’t tell you what the approach actually is. They won’t say what you are to do as a teacher to protect the rights of your students to learn without interference.
You can’t escape human nature. You can’t escape the fact that when enforcement is removed, the result is more misbehavior.

True accountability, wherein a misbehaving student misses out on something they want to be part of, is good. It teaches critical life lessons like responsibility, empathy, humility, respect, and the desire not to make the same mistake again.
Walk the halls in your fanciest suit, hold your chin up high, and look down your nose at those doing the noble work in the classrooms.
